\par In this section we will examine how Cartesian closed categories can be constructed out of more elemental categories, especially out of compact closed categories.
The latter are natural models of systems with a relational semantics, for instance electrical circuits, whereas the former are, as we have just seen, frameworks for models of programming languages.
``Compiling'' conventional programming languages into circuits is a long standing area of engineering interest, generally called \emph{high level synthesis}.
Indeed, this process can be achieved systematically by understanding how Cartesian closed categories can be constructed out of compact closed categories, a construction dubbed \emph{the Geometry of Synthesis}\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/popl/Ghica07}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
The name of the construction is a homage to a famous construction in semantics of linear logic proofs called \emph{the Geometry of Interaction}, which shows how compact closed categories arise out of traced monoidal categories \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:journals/mscs/AbramskyHS02}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} and which can also be given an intuitively diagrammatic construction.
\par We will describe it briefly, starting with the diagram language of compact closed categories, which are (symmetric for this case) monoidal categories such that every object $A$ has:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@a \emph{dual} $A^{*}$, unique up to canonical isomorphism;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a \emph{unit} $\eta_{A}:I\mapsto A^{*}\otimes A$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a \emph{counit} $\epsilon_{A}:A\otimes A^{*}\to A$
\end{itemize}represented diagramatically as:
$$\begin{picture}\put(-0.00459,0.09568){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\eta_{A}=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compactcc.pdf}}\put(0.55619,0.09223){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\epsilon_{A}=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compactcc.pdf}}\put(0.78355,0.17809){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A^{*}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.77872,0.01068){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.2627,0.18292){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.26667,0.01551){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A^{*}$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$such that the following equations hold, expressed directly in the diagrammatic language:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.14049,0.14851){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compactcceq.pdf}}\put(0.67754,0.1446){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.23538,0.00985){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.02569,0.17243){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.29236,0.27586){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compactcceq.pdf}}\put(0.84329,0.00827){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A^{*}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.75112,0.27429){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A^{*}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.57676,0.17492){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A^{*}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compactcceq.pdf}}\end{picture}$$Using the machinery of the (symmetric) compact closed category, a monoidal closed category can be constructed in a standard way:
$$\hskip 77.49976pt\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncc.pdf}}\put(0.19082,0.08132){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A^{*}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.30195,0.05582){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A^{*}\otimes B\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}A\multimap B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.04843,0.04342){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.19271,0.0317){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.11688,0.01978){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncc.pdf}}\put(0.00521,0.01985){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$Evaluation and the proof of correctness of evaluation (the $\beta$ law) are given below:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncceval.pdf}}\put(0.12092,0.08249){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncceval.pdf}}\put(0.12092,0.22088){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$g$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncceval.pdf}}\put(0.32171,0.00495){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{eval}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.10632,0.00495){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\Lambda(f)$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncceval.pdf}}\put(0.55842,0.08249){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncceval.pdf}}\put(0.55842,0.22088){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$g$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncceval.pdf}}\put(0.42806,0.12546){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.91259,0.12862){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncceval.pdf}}\put(0.78759,0.144){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$g$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncceval.pdf}}\put(0.6757,0.12515){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compcc2moncceval.pdf}}\end{picture}$$The first equation relies on strictifier/de-strictifier cancellation and symmetry.
The second equation is the `yanking' property of compact closed category in which the unit/co-unit pair cancel out, allowing the straightening of the wire.
\par However, this simple solution is not satisfactory because of a ``no go'' result of category theory, that in a compact closed category the product is automatically a co-product.
It is not important to dwell at this stage on what a co-product is, but having the two coincide is a degeneracy of the framework: in other words, there are now too many equations in the category, allowing certain constructions that should be distinct to be identified.
Therefore, this construction cannot be used to eliminate the need of a direct construction for a Cartesian closed category, as seen so far.
\par This construction is useful in the context of `high-level synthesis', with a caveat: the category cannot have unrestricted Cartesian product.
Restricting the scope of the product while maintaining the usefulness of the language require certain type-system trickery inspired by bounded linear logic, which is beyond the scope of this tutorial \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/popl/GhicaS11}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
\par\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Abstract syntax graphs}
\par\par This section is informal, intended to reconnect the readers, especially those less versed into category theoretical concepts, with more basic and more available intuitions.
As such, the section can be skipped without loss of continuity, especially by the reader confident in their mathematical intuitions.
\par It is common, especially in the area of compilers, to cling to the oversimplified view that syntax is represented by a \emph{tree}.
In fact, syntax is a far more sophisticated data structure: a \emph{hierarchical graph}.
In this section we shall see how the diagrams we used so far can be informally reconstructed as a data structure which enhances in a rather intuitive way the more commonly used yet often unsatisfactory `\emph{abstract syntax trees}' (AST).
\par As an expression of algebraic expressions, abstract syntax trees are perfectly adequate.
Consider an expression such as $1+(2+3)$.
Its tree representation is conventionally written top-to-bottom like this:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast.pdf}}\put(0.10674,0.42305){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$1$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast.pdf}}\put(0.32694,0.79004){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast.pdf}}\put(0.32694,0.05605){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$2$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast.pdf}}\put(0.76733,0.05605){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$3$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast.pdf}}\put(0.54713,0.42305){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast.pdf}}\end{picture}$$This syntax tree is `abstract' in the sense that not all the lexical tokens of the original are represented in the tree, namely the open and closed brackets in this example.
\par The representation becomes unsatisfactory when variables are introduced, as in the expression $x+(2+x)$.
The AST of this expression is:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2.pdf}}\put(0.10734,0.42541){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2.pdf}}\put(0.32877,0.79446){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2.pdf}}\put(0.32877,0.05637){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$2$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2.pdf}}\put(0.77163,0.05637){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2.pdf}}\put(0.55019,0.42541){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2.pdf}}\end{picture}$$The problem with this representation, as a data structure, is that it offers poor support to the most common operations performed on variables: substitution.
Replacing $x$ with, say, 0 requires searching the entire graph for occurrences of $x$.
By contrast, using string diagrams the same expression is represented such that only one logical occurrence of the variable $x$, the leftmost wire, is shared by two nodes in the expression:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2sd.pdf}}\put(0.25949,0.15758){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$2$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2sd.pdf}}\put(0.53536,0.05414){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2sd.pdf}}\put(0.81121,0.15758){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast2sd.pdf}}\end{picture}$$To perform a substitution we no longer require to search the tree for occurrences of $x$, as there is only a single occurrence of the variable.
In fact, in any reasonable concrete implementation of string diagrams the left and right interface wires need to be explicitly recorded, which makes substitution possible in constant time, relative to the size of the overall string diagram.
\par Once binding syntax is introduced, the shortcomings of the AST become more perspicuous.
Consider the expression $\mathit{let}\ x=0\ in\ x+(2+x)$.
The AST form of the expression is:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3.pdf}}\put(0.46364,0.25561){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3.pdf}}\put(0.59668,0.47736){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3.pdf}}\put(0.28624,0.69911){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{let}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3.pdf}}\put(0.59668,0.03387){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$2$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3.pdf}}\put(0.86278,0.03387){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3.pdf}}\put(0.72973,0.25561){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3.pdf}}\put(0.33059,0.47736){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$0$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3.pdf}}\put(0.06449,0.47736){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3.pdf}}\end{picture}$$Note that the binding occurrence of $x$ and the regular occurrence are not distinguished, and there is no easy way to connect them.
By contrast, the same expression, using a string diagram representation, is:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3sd.pdf}}\put(0.38819,0.1302){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$2$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3sd.pdf}}\put(0.04631,0.1302){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$0$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3sd.pdf}}\put(0.61611,0.04473){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3sd.pdf}}\put(0.84402,0.1302){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast3sd.pdf}}\end{picture}$$The overall structure is clearer, and it corresponds more closely to the \emph{meaning} of the expression.
The problem of relating variable occurrences to the binder is solved be making variables into wires rather than boxes.
This distinction between variables and operations is useful in several ways, perhaps the most important being that the string diagram is automatically quotiented by alpha equivalence.
\par The convenience of this approach becomes more perspicuous in the case of variable shadowing, as in
$$\mathit{let}\ x=0\ in\ (\mathit{let}\ x=1\ in\ x+2)+x$$The AST is of course not ambiguous, but connecting variable occurrences to their binders is even more difficult:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.73883,0.45562){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.61184,0.66727){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.2732,0.87892){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{let}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.61184,0.03233){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.86582,0.03233){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$2$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.73883,0.24397){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.31553,0.66727){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$0$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.06156,0.66727){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.44252,0.45562){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{let}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.48485,0.24397){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$1$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\put(0.23087,0.24397){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4.pdf}}\end{picture}$$This is why for purposes of mechanisation this representation of variables is usually avoided.
The more streamlined, if harder for human consumption, notation of deBruijn indices is the preferred alternative.
The string diagram representation of this expression is easy to read and it avoids all the pitfalls of variable shadowing:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4sd.pdf}}\put(0.35122,0.2287){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$2$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4sd.pdf}}\put(0.0491,0.37976){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$0$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4sd.pdf}}\put(0.20016,0.04743){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$1$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4sd.pdf}}\put(0.59291,0.13807){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4sd.pdf}}\put(0.83459,0.2287){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ast4sd.pdf}}\end{picture}$$The rather remarkable thing to note here is that this string diagram is \emph{equal} to that of just $(1+2)+0$!
So the string diagram notation is significantly more abstract than `abstract' syntax trees, as not just alpha equivalence but also linear substitution are absorbed in the notation.
\par The version of string diagrams used up to this point can be called, in their concrete representation, `abstract syntax DAGs' (directed acyclic graphs).
The hierarchical aspect appears with the introduction of \emph{thunks}.
Categorical considerations aside, thunks are have uses both semantically and syntactically.
Semantically they indicate to the evaluator that the evaluation of a piece of code must be postponed; first, a thunk needs to be `forced', i.e. extracted from its protective bubble, by some other operations.
We have already seen how the if-then-else statement forces one of its argument thunks and how application forces the thunk that corresponds to the applied function.
\par Representing the nullary (i.e. which binds zero variables) thunks of the if-then-else statement explicitly may not seem justified enough.
But the small notational overhead of indicating the thunk explicitly is relevant for generic analyses that want to take the flow of control into account, as the presence of the thunk immediately indicates that the program can control and direct the evaluation.
But these are rather subtle and partly manufactured reasons; the real reasons are conceptual, the consistency and integrity of the string diagram notation, as presented in the previous sections.
\par A more direct case can be made for the hierarchical notation in the case of thunks which also bind variables, as is the case with functions.
Taking the ubiquitous $\lambda$-abstraction, the same issues of binding and alpha equivalence discuss earlier will come into play again.
Notably, the binding structures above did not involve thunks.
Why do we need thunks for $\lambda$ and why is the hierarchical structure a reasonable evolution of the AST?
\par The most important thing is that thunks must be seen as undivided whole, in particular when it comes to their interaction with the Cartesian equations for copying and discarding.
Let us illustrate this with a simple non-example, in which we attempt, and fail, to represent thunks without resorting to hierarchical structure: $\lambda x.x+x$.
The conventional AST we have already agreed that it is not ideal, so we will use the variable conventions of string diagrams while treating the $\lambda$ as if it were an operation:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam.pdf}}\put(0.11515,0.33059){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\lambda$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam.pdf}}\put(0.11515,0.07208){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam.pdf}}\put(0.27026,0.07208){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam.pdf}}\put(0.1927,0.20133){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam.pdf}}\put(0.03759,0.20133){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$x$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam.pdf}}\put(0.76143,0.33059){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\lambda$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam.pdf}}\put(0.83899,0.20133){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam.pdf}}\end{picture}$$This is an approach similar to that taken in \emph{Interaction nets}.
\par But this notation is clearly problematic both in the presence of copy and discard operation.
A term such as $\mathit{let}\ f=\lambda x.x\ in\ f\,f$ is represented in a way that applying the copying axioms results in an ill-formed string diagram which corresponds to no legal term:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam2.pdf}}\put(0.08705,0.32226){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\lambda$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam2.pdf}}\put(0.03024,0.58434){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{apply}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam2.pdf}}\put(0.60984,0.58434){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{apply}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam2.pdf}}\put(0.16265,0.19626){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam2.pdf}}\put(0.56585,0.42306){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\lambda$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam2.pdf}}\put(0.64145,0.19626){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam2.pdf}}\put(0.76745,0.42306){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\lambda$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam2.pdf}}\end{picture}$$To overcome this problem interaction nets uses a different kind of node when $\lambda$ nodes are duplicated, with $C$ for copy and $\delta$ as the special node resulting from the copying of a $\lambda$, so the copying rule for abstraction is:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlam3b.pdf}}\put(0.06726,0.33018){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.56497,0.08112){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\delta$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0674,0.21939){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\lambda$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.54013,0.33181){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\lambda$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.7621,0.33181){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\lambda$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.73366,0.07976){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\delta$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$This, however, is not a satisfactory solution since it ruins the naturality of copying.
The hierarchical graph structure prevents this problem by treating a thunk as a single indivisible thing.
Indeed, a thunk is always a node, with the inner graph its label:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlamsd.pdf}}\put(0.24858,0.09761){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{apply}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlamsd.pdf}}\put(0.11,0.09555){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlamsd.pdf}}\put(0.44141,0.09374){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlamsd.pdf}}\put(0.7479,0.09761){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{apply}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlamsd.pdf}}\put(0.62093,0.14199){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlamsd.pdf}}\put(0.62093,0.03361){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{astlamsd.pdf}}\end{picture}$$\begin{exercise}Consider the way in which applying the discard equation is not compatible with the naive representation of $\lambda$ nodes are operations.
\end{exercise}\par Before we conclude, a note on expressing the the beta law or, more generally, the unit-counit cancellation in string diagrams.
The widely used string diagrams for strict monoidal compact closed categories absorb the cancellation rule for adjunctions.
Without going into the technical detail, the unit and the co-unit can be represented as `loops' so that their cancellation equations
\@@amsgather
have neat topological interpretations:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compact-closed.pdf}}\put(0.76596,0.08452){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.60004,0.19523){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathrm{id}_{A^{*}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compact-closed.pdf}}\put(0.67646,0.01182){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathrm{id}_{A^{*}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.62056,0.04738){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\eta$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.70615,0.12381){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\epsilon$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.83856,0.10352){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathrm{id}_{A^{*}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compact-closed.pdf}}\put(0.16986,0.08452){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.07731,0.19523){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathrm{id}_{A}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compact-closed.pdf}}\put(0.01311,0.01182){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathrm{id}_{A}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.02446,0.13298){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\eta$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.11005,0.03821){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\epsilon$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.24246,0.10352){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathrm{id}_{A}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{compact-closed.pdf}}\end{picture}$$Such notations do not seem to be readily available for the unit/co-unit pair involved in the beta law.
A notable attempt has been made by Baez and Stay, who proposed a `bubble'-`claps' pair in their seminal `Rosetta Stone' paper.
However, their proposal was informal, a side issue to the main thrust of their paper, which focusses on the compact closed structure.
We will attempt to refine our notation here to make it more similar to bubble-clasp diagrams, but only for the sake of explanation.
In the sequel we will use the graphical syntactic sugar already introduced.
\par Currying in the Rosetta notation, vs. our notation is:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-currying.pdf}}\put(0.50276,0.05445){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$X$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.66806,0.09577){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$Y$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-currying.pdf}}\put(0.50533,0.10967){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.72359,0.09567){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$X\multimap Y$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-currying.pdf}}\put(0.60377,0.07315){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-currying.pdf}}\put(0.40102,0.09177){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}vs.\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.31276,0.00605){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$X$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.31301,0.11146){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$Y$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-currying.pdf}}\put(0.03873,0.12536){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-currying.pdf}}\put(0.13717,0.08884){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-currying.pdf}}\end{picture}$$We can see that this notation is trying to maintain the strict monoidal convention that each wire is labelled by an object, so that composite wires can be decomposed in their constituents.
However, in the case of closed monoidal structure it is not a good idea to give direct access to both $X$ and $Y$ separately in $X\multimap Y$ unless additional graphical conventions are used to prevent nonsensical use of the clasp.
\par The Rosetta notation `peeks' inside the evaluation, so that the beta law is written as the following string diagram equation.
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-beta.pdf}}\put(0.29122,0.08218){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$X$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.2915,0.21111){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$Y$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-beta.pdf}}\put(0.04276,0.21012){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-beta.pdf}}\put(0.15142,0.16981){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-beta.pdf}}\put(0.40576,0.00544){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{eval}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-beta.pdf}}\put(0.53284,0.10862){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-beta.pdf}}\put(0.58835,0.07257){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$X$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.83741,0.19522){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$Y$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-beta.pdf}}\put(0.58867,0.21056){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-beta.pdf}}\put(0.73754,0.17025){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rosetta-beta.pdf}}\end{picture}$$This is graphically more compelling as it establishes a visual parallel with the way compact closed categories cancel out the two adjunctions.
By using the clasp in a way similar to the strictifier/de-strictifier morphisms, and by pairing it with an `anti-clasp' we can combine our notation with the Rosetta in a way that is perhaps graphically more informative without raising the possibility of ill-formed diagrams:

the clasps and the anti-clasp now ruin somewhat the visual appeal.
But this is the price we may need to pay to avoid ill-formed diagrams.
The additional purchase of the clasps is not worth the additional clutter, so we will stick to the simpler notation.
The reader who disagrees may adopt it, with no cost in terms of rigour.
\par We conclude here this brief and informal section.
In it we have temporarily suspended our category-theory-driven approach and attempted to persuade the reader that string diagrams, and their concrete incarnation as hierarchical abstract syntax graphs (or more precisely abstract syntax DAGs) could be recovered as an evolution of the more conventional AST representation in which variables, binding, sharing, copying, and discarding are dealt with in such a way so that many useful properties are absorbed in the notation.
\par\par\par\par\lx@newpage\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{String Diagram Rewriting}
\par\par\par Even though we specified the reduction rules of the $\lambda$ calculus as equations, they display a clear directionality. For instance, the $\beta$ rule may be seen as the process of applying a term $\lambda x.u$ to a value $v$, resulting into the term $u[v/x]$. More formally, this amounts to orienting the equation $(\lambda x.u)=u[v/x]$ into a \emph{rewrite rule} $(\lambda x.u)v\rightsquigarrow u[v/x]$. We may apply such a rule inside a $\lambda$-term $t$ when the left-hand side $(\lambda x.u)v$ appears as a sub-term of $t$ --- in this case say that $t$ contains a \emph{redex} for the rewrite rule. Applying the rule then results into the substitution of $(\lambda x.u)v$ with $u[v/x]$ inside $t$.
\par The rewriting theory of the $\lambda$ calculus is fundamental to describe the computational behaviour of $\lambda$-terms via an \emph{operational semantics} --- a perspective that we will pursue in Section\penalty\ \ref{sec:oslc} below. The subject of this section is to illustrate how rewriting works when applied to string diagrams rather than terms.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Rewriting of string diagrams in symmetric monoidal categories}
\par We first consider the case of string diagrams in a symmetric strict monoidal category, as introduced in Section\penalty\ \ref{sec:sdssmc}. A naive attempt of transposing the above definitions to the context of string diagrammatic syntax poses immediate challenges. Consider the following example. Suppose we have a rewrite rule of string diagrams

\par\begin{equation}{\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\put(0.78629,0.09794){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$g$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00543,0.29659){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00756,0.07275){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.89545,0.29339){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\put(0.23421,0.27024){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\put(0.41765,0.15822){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$i$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\put(0.90713,0.13564){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0072,0.18254){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\end{picture}}.\end{equation}`Morally', $t$ contains a redex for the rule. But, strictly speaking, we can isolate the left-hand side of the rule as a sub-term of $t$ only if we first use naturality of the symmetry (Figure\penalty\ \ref{fig:eqsym}) to rearrange $t$ into a string diagram $t^{\prime}$, as follows:
\begin{equation}\raisebox{-19.91684pt}{\hbox{\scalebox{.75}{\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\put(0.78629,0.09794){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$g$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00543,0.29659){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00756,0.07275){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.89545,0.29339){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\put(0.23421,0.27024){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\put(0.41765,0.15822){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$i$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\put(0.90713,0.13564){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0072,0.18254){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagrewlhs.pdf}}\end{picture}}}}\quad=\quad\raisebox{-19.91684pt}{\scalebox{.75}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ruleappLHS.pdf}}\put(0.43171,0.22089){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$g$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00661,0.30399){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00881,0.07246){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.90404,0.24776){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular $t$ and $t^{\prime}$ in\penalty\ \eqref{eq:rearrangeforrew} are equivalent modulo the laws of symmetric monoidal categories. We now have a clear indication of how to apply the rewrite rule: simply replace in $t^{\prime}$ the left-hand side of the rule with its right-hand side:
\begin{equation}\raisebox{-19.91684pt}{\scalebox{.75}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ruleappLHS.pdf}}\put(0.43171,0.22089){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$g$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00661,0.30399){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00881,0.07246){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.90404,0.24776){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ruleappLHS.pdf}}\put(0.24325,0.27674){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ruleappLHS.pdf}}\put(0.63314,0.03599){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$i$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ruleappLHS.pdf}}\put(0.90179,0.06144){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00844,0.18602){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ruleappLHS.pdf}}\end{picture}}}}\quad\rightsquigarrow\quad\raisebox{-19.91684pt}{\scalebox{.75}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ruleappRHS.pdf}}\put(0.24281,0.22341){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$h$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00661,0.30399){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.00881,0.07246){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.90404,0.24776){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smas example suggests that the notion of redex becomes way subtler once moving from terms to string diagrams. A string diagram is an equivalence class of terms, and to find a redex in a string diagrams means to find at least one member of such an equivalence class which contains a redex in the traditional sense. More formally:
\par\begin{definition}Consider a rewrite rule $$\mathcal{R}\qquad=\qquad\ \raisebox{-5.69046pt}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagl.pdf}}\put(0.70601,0.2174){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.38836,0.13508){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$l$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.06336,0.19838){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}}}\rightsquigarrow\ \raisebox{-5.69046pt}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagr.pdf}}\put(0.70601,0.2174){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.38836,0.13508){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$r$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.06336,0.19838){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}}}.$$We say that a string diagram \ \raisebox{-5.69046pt}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.69214,0.20709){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$D$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.04871,0.20839){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\put(0.38655,0.12145){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\end{picture}}} has a \emph{redex} for the rule $\mathcal{R}$ if there exist string diagrams

\begin{equation*}\ \raisebox{-5.69046pt}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.69214,0.20709){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$D$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.04871,0.20839){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\put(0.38655,0.12145){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\end{picture}}}\quad=\quad\raisebox{-14.22636pt}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rewcontextLHS.pdf}}\put(0.26507,0.18808){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rewcontextLHS.pdf}}\put(0.4126,0.05558){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$Q$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.14603,0.09887){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$l_{C}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.01304,0.12748){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rewcontextLHS.pdf}}\put(0.88272,0.13392){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$D$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.76146,0.09805){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$r_{C}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.60617,0.18445){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rewcontextLHS.pdf}}\put(0.46209,0.15193){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$l$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}}}\end{equation*}modulo the laws of symmetric monoidal categories. If $\ \raisebox{-5.69046pt}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.69214,0.20709){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$D$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.04871,0.20839){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\put(0.38655,0.12145){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\end{picture}}}$ has such a redex, then rewriting $\ \raisebox{-5.69046pt}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.69214,0.20709){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$D$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.04871,0.20839){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\put(0.38655,0.12145){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\end{picture}}}$ with $\mathcal{R}$ produces
\begin{equation*}\ \raisebox{-5.69046pt}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.69214,0.20709){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$D$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.04871,0.20839){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\put(0.38655,0.12145){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$f$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{diagf.pdf}}\end{picture}}}\quad\rightsquigarrow\quad\raisebox{-14.22636pt}{\hbox{\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rewcontextRHS.pdf}}\put(0.26507,0.18808){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$A$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rewcontextRHS.pdf}}\put(0.4126,0.05558){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$Q$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.14603,0.09887){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$l_{C}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.01304,0.12748){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$C$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rewcontextRHS.pdf}}\put(0.88272,0.13392){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$D$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.76146,0.09805){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$r_{C}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.60617,0.18445){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rewcontextRHS.pdf}}\put(0.45094,0.16308){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$r$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}}}\end{equation*}\end{definition}Although mathematically correct, this definition of string diagram rewriting is unsatisfactory from a practical viewpoint. If we aim at studying the operational behaviour of programs using rewriting, finding a redex should be a computationally feasible task. When it amounts to finding a sub-term inside a $\lambda$-term, this is the case. However, imagine searching for a redex in a string diagram: one would need to explore the space of all equivalent terms represented by such diagram, trying to find one with a redex. This is typically an extremely expensive process to implement.
\par For this reason, we need to rely on an interpretation of string diagrams which is more efficient for the purpose of rewriting. The data structure which we use to interpret string diagrams is the one of a \emph{open hypergraph}.
\par In a nutshell, open hypergraphs generalise standard (directed) graphs in two ways. First, edges are replaced with \emph{hyperedges}: whereas an edge has just one ingoing and one outgoing node, a hyperedge may have multiple of them (or none), organised as lists. Second, the structures we consider are `open', in the sense that some of their nodes act as an \emph{interface}, with which they may be combined together with other hypergraphs. Thanks to the interface, open hypergraphs may mirror sequential and parallel composition of string diagrams, and are thus adapted to interpret them.
\par An example showing our graphical representation of open hypergraphs is displayed in\penalty\ \eqref{ex:hyp} below. First, we proceed with the formal definition of these structures. Labels for nodes and hyperedges will come from a \emph{monoidal signature}, as introduced in Section\penalty\ \ref{sec:smc} when discussing freely generated symmetric strict monoidal categories.
\par\begin{definition}Fix a monoidal signature $\Sigma=(\Sigma_{0},\Sigma_{1})$ of objects $\Sigma_{0}$ and morphisms $\Sigma_{1}$. A \emph{($\Sigma$-labelled) hypergraph} is a tuple $(N,E,v,l_{n},l_{e},)$ where
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@$N$ is a set of nodes
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$E$ is a set of hyperedges
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$v\colon E\to N^{\star}\times N^{\star}$ is a function assigning to each hyperedge $e$ a list $\pi_{1}(v(e))$ of ingoing nodes and a list $\pi_{2}(v(e))$ of outogoing nodes
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$l_{n}\colon N\to\Sigma_{0}$ is a function labelling each node with a generating object in $\Sigma_{0}$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$l_{e}\colon E\to\Sigma_{1}$ is a function labelling each hyperedge with a generating object in $\Sigma_{0}$, with the requirement that $l_{e}(e)$ must have arity $\pi_{1}(v(e))$ and coarity $\pi_{2}(v(e))$ in $\Sigma_{0}$.
\end{itemize}Given $\Sigma$-labelled hypergraphs $G=(N,E,v,l_{n},l_{e},)$ and $G^{\prime}=(N^{\prime},E^{\prime},v^{\prime},{l^{\prime}}_{n},{l^{\prime}}_{e},)$, a \emph{hypergraph morphism} $f\colon G\to G^{\prime}$ consists of functions $f_{N}\colon N\to N^{\prime}$ and $f_{E}\colon E\to E^{\prime}$ respecting the labelling of nodes and hyperedges and the type of hyperedges. In other words, ${l^{\prime}}_{n}(f_{N}(n))=v(n)$, ${l^{\prime}}_{e}(f_{E}(e))=l_{e}(e)$, and $v^{\prime}(f_{E}(e))=(\hat{f}_{N}(\pi_{1}(v(e)),\hat{f}_{N}(\pi_{2}(v(e)))$, where $\hat{f}_{N}\colon N^{\star}\to N^{\star}$ is the lifting of $f_{N}\colon N\to N^{\prime}$, defined point-wise in the obvious way. Such a morphism is a \emph{monomorphism} if $f_{N}$ and $f_{E}$ are both injective functions.
\par A ($\Sigma$-labelled) \emph{open} hypergraph is a tuple $(L,G,R,f_{L},f_{R})$ where
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@$G$ is a $\Sigma$-labelled hypergraph, called the \emph{carrier}
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$L$ is a discrete $\Sigma$-labelled hypergraph, called the \emph{left interface} of $G$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$R$ is a discrete $\Sigma$-labelled hypergraph, called the \emph{right interface} of $G$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$f_{L}\colon L\to G$ and $f_{R}\colon R\to G$ are hypergraph morphisms.
\end{itemize}A \emph{open hypergraph morphism} $h\colon(L,G,R,f_{L},f_{R})\to(L^{\prime},G^{\prime},R^{\prime},f^{\prime}_{L},f^{\prime}_{R})$ consists of hypergraph morphisms $h_{G}\colon G\to G^{\prime}$, $h_{L}\colon L\to L^{\prime}$, $h_{R}\colon R\to R^{\prime}$ commuting with the interface morphisms, i.e. such that $h_{L}\mathbin{;}f^{\prime}_{L}=f_{L}\mathbin{;}h_{G}$ and $h_{R}\mathbin{;}f^{\prime}_{R}=f_{R}\mathbin{;}h_{G}$.
\end{definition}\par\begin{example}Fix $\Sigma=(\{A,B,C\},\{f\colon A\otimes B\to C\},g\colon C\to B\})$. Here is an example of open $\Sigma$-hypergraph $(G,L,R,f_{L},f_{R})$, displayed both as a tuple (top) and in its graphical representation --- in\penalty\ \eqref{ex:hyp} below.

\end{example}\par\par As mentioned, the presence of interfaces is essential to be able to \emph{compose} open hypergraphs sequentially, mimicking the way string diagrams are composed. Given open hypergraphs $H_{1}=(L_{1},G_{1},R_{1},f_{L_{1}},f_{R_{1}})$ and $H_{2}=L_{2},G_{2},R_{2},f_{L_{2}},f_{R_{2}})$ such that $R_{1}=L_{2}$, we can form a composite open hypergraph $H_{1}\mathbin{;}H_{2}=(L_{1},G,R_{2},f^{\prime}_{L_{1}},f_{R_{2}})$, where $G$ has been obtained by `gluing' together $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ along the common interface $R_{1}=L_{2}$. For instance:
\@@amsgather
This operation can be defined in full generality using category theory. $\Sigma$-labelled hypergraphs form a category, in which open hypergraphs $H_{1}$ and $H_{2}$ as above can be identified with \emph{cospans} $L_{1}\xrightarrow{f_{L_{1}}}G_{1}\xleftarrow{f_{R_{1}}}R_{1}$ and $L_{2}\xrightarrow{f_{L_{2}}}G_{2}\xleftarrow{f_{R_{2}}}R_{2}$ respectively. The composite open hypergraph $H_{1}\mathbin{;}H_{2}$ is then defined by the cospan $L_{1}\xrightarrow{f_{L_{1}}\mathbin{;}p_{1}}G\xleftarrow{f_{R_{2}}\mathbin{;}p_{2}}R_{2}$ obtained via pushout along the shared interface $R_{1}=L_{2}$:
\par\par\@@eqnarray
Moreover, we can easily define a monoidal product operation between open hypergraphs of arbitrary interfaces, which pictorially amounts to stacking them vertically. For instance, with $H_{1}$ and $H_{2}$ as above, we have:
\par\@@eqnarray
\par\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\par The reason to introduce open hypergraphs is that there is a well-behaved, natural interpretation of string diagrams into them. In a nutshell, each box (morphism) of a string diagram corresponds to a hyperedge, and each wire (object) corresponds to a node. Nodes on the interfaces correspond to the domain (left interface) and the codomain (right interface) of the string diagram. Sequential and parallel composition of string diagrams is interpreted as composition of open hypergraphs by $\mathbin{;}$ and $\otimes$ respectively, as defined above.
\par\par\begin{definition}Let $\Sigma$ be a signature. We define inductively an interpretation $[\![\cdot]\!]$ mapping symmetric monoidal $\Sigma$-terms into $\Sigma$-labelled open hypergraphs as follows:
\@@amsgather
\end{definition}Note the interpretation is defined inductively on terms, but it is perfectly valid on string diagrams, because any two terms that are equal modulo the laws of symmetric monoidal categories are mapped to the same open hypergraph. In fact, even though we introduced this interpretation primarily for the purpose of implementing string diagram rewriting, it is of independent interest: in Section\penalty\ \ref{sec:sdssmc}, we first introduced string diagrams as \emph{syntactic} object, but we now have a formal justification to reason about them \emph{combinatorially}, through the lenses of their hypergraph interpretation.
\par\par\begin{example}The following string diagram, on the same signature $\Sigma$ considered in Example\penalty\ \ref{ex:hypergraph}, is mapped via $[\![\cdot]\!]$ onto the open hypergraph of equation\penalty\ \eqref{ex:hyp}.

}}\end{gathered}\end{equation}In these open hypergraphs, nodes deviate from their standard behaviour in the string diagram interpretation. In the first example, one node appears twice on the left interface. In the second example, one node does not appear on the right interface, even though it has no outgoing link to any hyperedge. In the third example, the same node is linked twice to the same hyperedge.
\par Inspired by these examples, we may give a general characterisation of precisely which open hypergraphs are in the image of the interpretation.
\begin{definition}An open hypergraph \\
$(G,L,R,f_{L},f_{R})$ is monogamous if
\begin{enumerate}\enumerate@item@$f_{L}$ and $f_{R}$ are monomorphisms of hypergraphs
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@for all nodes $n\in N$ of $G=(N,E,v,l_{n},l_{e})$:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@If $n$ is in the image of $f_{L}$, $n$ is not an outgoing node of any hyperedge, i.e. $n\not\in\pi_{2}(v(e))$ for all $e\in E$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@If $n$ is in the image of $f_{R}$, $n$ is not an ingoing node of any hyperedge, i.e. $n\not\in\pi_{1}(v(e))$ for all $e\in E$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Otherwise, $n$ is not in the above images. In this case, $n$ must be an outgoing node of exactly one hyperedge $e$ and an ingoing node of exactly one hyperedge $e^{\prime}$.
\end{itemize}\end{enumerate}\end{definition}\par Intuitively, monogamicity ensures that nodes on the left/right interface cannot be linked on the same side to a hyperedge, and nodes not on the interface are linked exactly to two hyperedges, one on their left and one on their right. For instance, the first open hypergraph in\penalty\ \eqref{eq:nonmonogamous} is not monogamous because its left interface morphism $f_{L}$ is not a monomorphism. The second is not monogamous because a node is not on any interface but it is linked to no hyperedge on its right. Finally, the third is not monogamous because a node is not on any interface but it is linked more than once to hyperedges on its left (the fact that it is linked to the same hyperedge twice or to different ones is immaterial to the criterion).
\par\par\begin{theorem}An open hypergraph is monogamous if and only if it is in the image of the interpretation $[\![\cdot]\!]$.
\end{theorem}\begin{proof}One direction is straightforward: by induction on $\Sigma$-terms we can verify that, if an open hypergraph is in the image of $[\![\cdot]\!]$, then it is monogamous. The converse direction requires more work: it amounts to show that any monogamous open hypergraph can be factorised as the composite of `atomic' open hypergraph, where each is either in the image of a structural $\Sigma$-term (identity or symmetry) or of a generating morphism in $\Sigma_{1}$. Working out the general case of this lemma, albeit not conceptually deep, is laborious: we refer to the literature in Section\penalty\ \ref{sec:relatedwork-rewriting} for a full proof. Here we confine ourselves to an example:

}}$$\end{proof}\par Having introduced open hypergraphs and explained their correspondence with string diagrams, we are ready to turn to our initial question: rewriting. From the purpose of rewriting, the fundamental appeal of the interpretation $[\![\cdot]\!]$ is that, whereas a string diagram represents an equivalence class of terms, we can reason about the corresponding open hypergraph as a single entity. In other words, the interpretation $[\![\cdot]\!]$ `absorbs' all the laws of symmetric monoidal categories, allowing us to forego any consideration about equivalence when inspecting the subparts of these objects in search of a redex. We can encapsulate this observation as the following lemma.
\par\begin{lemma}A string diagram $c$ has a redex for a rule $l\rightsquigarrow r$ in the sense of Definition\penalty\ \ref{def:rewritestepsyn} if and only if the carrier of the open hypergraph $[\![c]\!]$ contains the carrier of $[\![l]\!]$ as a convex sub-hypergraph.
\end{lemma}\par Before turning attention to the proof of this lemma, there is one notion that needs clarification: convexity.
\par\begin{definition}A \emph{path} $p$ from a hyperedge $e$ to a hyperedge $e^{\prime}$ in a hypergraph $G=(N,E,v,l_{n},l_{e})$ is a sequence $e_{1},\dots,e_{n}$ of hyperedges such that $e_{1}=e$, $e_{n}=e^{\prime}$, and $\pi_{2}(v(e_{i}))\cap\pi_{1}(v(e_{i+1}))\neq\emptyset$ for all $i$ with $1\leq i\leq n$. In other words, each hyperedge $e_{i}$ in the path is linked to $e_{i+1}$ via at least one node, which is outgoing of $e_{i}$ and ingoing to $e_{i+1}$.
\par A sub-hypergraph $H$ of $G$ is \emph{convex} if, for any nodes $n,n^{\prime}$ in $H$ and any path $p$ from $n$ to $n^{\prime}$, every hyperedge in $p$ is also in $H$.
\end{definition}\par\par Intuitively, convexity ensures that a sub-hypergraph $H$ of $G$ has no `gaps'.

}}\end{equation*}\end{example}\par\par We have thus established that, in order to find a redex for a rule in string diagram rewriting, it suffices to inspect the corresponding open hypergraphs. How do we rewrite with them though? There is a long tradition in graph rewriting of using ``double-pushout'' (DPO) constructions in the category of graphs in order to formally define rewriting of these structures. It turns out we can sensibly define a notion of DPO rewriting in the category of open hypergraphs, called `convex DPO rewriting with interfaces' (CDPOI), and make it correspond precisely to string diagram rewriting.
\par\begin{theorem}Let $l\rightsquigarrow r$ be a string diagram rewrite rule, and $t$ a string diagram on the same signature. Then $t$ rewrites into $t^{\prime}$ with rule $l\rightsquigarrow r$ in the sense of Definition\penalty\ \ref{def:rewritestepsyn} if and only if $[\![t]\!]$ rewrites into $[\![t^{\prime}]\!]$ with rule $[\![l]\!]\rightsquigarrow[\![r]\!]$ via CDPOI rewriting.
\end{theorem}\par\begin{example}We give a sense of the theorem via an example. The rewriting step\penalty\ \eqref{eq:rewstepstringdiag} is interpreted to the following CDPOI rewriting step.
\begin{equation*}\scalebox{0.7}{{\hbox to438.47pt{\vbox to285.53pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 221.00888pt\lower-156.99017pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \hbox to0.0pt{

}}\end{equation*}The top row features the left-hand side of the rewrite rule (left), its right-hand side (right), and their interface (center). In the middle row we have $[\![t]\!]$ (left) and the result of rewriting it via the rule (right). At the centre, the pushout complement: $[\![t]\!]$ with a `hole' replacing the redex subgraph. The redex itself is identified by the morphism $F$. The bottom row is occupied by the interface: its preservation during rewriting is ensured by commutativity of the diagram --- in which, moreover, the two squares are pushouts.
\end{example}\par There are a few subtleties involved in the theorem, namely on how CDPOI ensures soundness of hypergraph rewriting with respect to string diagram rewriting - a property which is not guaranteed by standard DPO rewriting. We do not elaborate on the precise definition of CDPOI rewriting, nor on the proof of the theorem, as that would bring us too far from the focus of this tutorial. The interested reader is referred to Section\penalty\ \ref{sec:relatedwork-rewriting} below for pointers to the relevant literature.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Rewriting of hierarchical string diagrams}
\par As seen in Section\penalty\ \ref{sec:hsdcmc}, higher-order computation may be modelled by moving from string diagrams, living in SMCs, to hierarchical string diagrams, living in SCMCs. How does rewriting theory extend to such setting? The key step is to identify a generalisation of hypergraphs suitable for modelling the layered structure of hierarchical string diagrams. This leads to the notion of (open) \emph{hierarchical hypergraph}. Labels for these structures come from closed monoidal signatures, see Definition\penalty\ \ref{def:freeSCMC}.
\par\begin{definition}Fix a closed monoidal signature $\Sigma=(\Sigma_{0},\Sigma_{1})$ of objects $\Sigma_{0}$ and morphisms $\Sigma_{1}$. A \emph{($\Sigma$-labelled) hierarchical hypergraph} is a $\Sigma$-labelled hypergraph $(N,E,v,l^{\prime}_{n},l^{\prime}_{e})$ together with a pair $(p_{E},p_{V})$ of functions where
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@$l^{\prime}_{n}\colon N\to obj_{\Sigma_{0}}$ extends the usual node labelling function with the possibility of assigning arbitrary objects in $obj_{\Sigma_{0}}$, instead of just the ones in $\Sigma_{0}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$l^{\prime}_{e}\colon E\to\Sigma_{1}\cup\{\bot\}$ extends the usual hyperedge labelling function with the possibility of assigning no label to a hyperedge --- i.e. the case $l^{\prime}_{e}(f)=\bot$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$v\colon E\to N^{\star}\times N^{\star}$ is a function assigning to each hyperedge $e$ a list $\pi_{1}(v(e))$ of ingoing nodes and a list $\pi_{2}(v(e))$ of outogoing nodes
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$p_{N}\colon N\to E+\{\bot\}$ and $p_{E}\colon E\to E+\{\bot\}$ assign to each node and hyperedge a `parent' hyperedge, or no parent ($\bot$)
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$p_{N}$ and $p_{E}$ satisfy the following constraints: (i) for each $e\in E$, each ingoing and outgoing node of $e$ must have the same parent as $e$ itself; (ii) the parent relation must be acyclic, in the sense that $(p_{E,\bot})^{k}(e)=\bot$ for some $k\geq 1$, where $p_{E,\bot}\colon E+1\to E+1$ is just the extension of $p_{E}$ adding $p_{E,\bot}(\bot)=\bot$.
\end{itemize}A \emph{morphism} between hierarchical hypergraphs $G=(N,E,v,l_{n},l_{e},p_{E},p_{V})$ and $G^{\prime}=(N^{\prime},E^{\prime},v^{\prime},l^{\prime}_{n},l^{\prime}_{e},p^{\prime}_{E},p^{\prime}_{V})$ is a hypergraph morphism $(f_{N}\colon N\to N^{\prime},f_{E}\colon E\to E^{\prime})$ respecting the hierarchical structure of $G$, in the following sense:
\@@eqnarray
A ($\Sigma$-labelled) \emph{open} hierarchical hypergraph is a tuple $(L,G,R,f_{L},f_{R})$ where
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@$G$ is a $\Sigma$-labelled hierarchical hypergraph, called the \emph{carrier}
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$L$ is a discrete $\Sigma$-labelled hierarchical hypergraph, called the \emph{left interface} of $G$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$R$ is a discrete $\Sigma$-labelled hierarchical hypergraph, called the \emph{right interface} of $G$
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$f_{L}\colon L\to G$ and $f_{R}\colon R\to G$ are hierarchical hypergraph morphisms.
\end{itemize}A \emph{open hierarchical hypergraph morphism} $h\colon(L,G,R,f_{L},f_{R})\to(L^{\prime},G^{\prime},R^{\prime},f^{\prime}_{L},f^{\prime}_{R})$ consists of hierarchical hypergraph morphisms $h_{G}\colon G\to G^{\prime}$, $h_{L}\colon L\to L^{\prime}$, $h_{R}\colon R\to R^{\prime}$ commuting with the interface morphisms, i.e. such that $h_{L}\mathbin{;}f^{\prime}_{L}=f_{L}\mathbin{;}h_{G}$ and $h_{R}\mathbin{;}f^{\prime}_{R}=f_{R}\mathbin{;}h_{G}$. \end{definition}\par In essence, a hierarchical hypergraph is a hypergraph with layers. In the above definition, layers are determined by the parent-child relation. The `outermost' layer $0$ is formed by those nodes and hyperedges that have no parent (i.e., their parent is $\bot$). Nodes and hyperedges in layer $n+1$ are those with parent hyperedge sitting in layer $n$.
\par Graphically, we may represent an open hierarchical hypergraph using `bubbles' to indicate layers, in a way that echoes the notation of hierarchical string diagrams. Here is an example.

}}\end{equation}\par Note layer borders cannot `cross' links between nodes and hyperedges, because of constraint (i) in the definition. The open hierarchical hypergraph in\penalty\ \eqref{eq:exhierarchicalhyp} has three hyperedges; two are labelled with $f$ and $g$ respectively, whereas the third is unlabelled (labelled with $\bot$). Note the unlabelled hyperedge has one ingoing node, labeled with $A$, and one outgoing node, labeled with $B\multimap B$. As for layers, the unlabelled hyperedge and $f$-labeled hyperedge have no parent and thus sit in layer $0$ (they are outermost). The unlabelled hyperedge is parent of the hyperedge labelled $g$ (and its sources and targets), which thus sits in layer $1$. We signal the different layers by depicting the $g$-labelled hyperedge inside the unlabelled one: this notation echoes the bubble operation in hierarchical string diagrams.
\par As for the interfaces, in open hierarchical hypergraphs we distinguish an \emph{outer} interface, which consists of the nodes on the left/right interface that sit in layer $0$. However, contrarily to standard hypergraphs, they may also have \emph{inner} interfaces, given by the nodes on the interfaces that sit in layers $n>0$. In\penalty\ \eqref{eq:exhierarchicalhyp} we use a vertical dotted line to separate the nodes of the layer $0$ interface from the nodes of the layer $1$ interface, and red/blue colouring for the interface maps to emphasise the different layers. In general, nodes of the inner interfaces are easily recognisable as they are the `dangling wires' of the hyperedges inside bubbles. In fact, for each unlabelled hyperedge $f$ we may distinguish an \emph{input interface}, given by nodes that have $f$ as parent and are in the left interface of the whole hypergraph, and an \emph{output interface}, given by nodes that have $f$ as parent and are in the right interface of the whole hypergraph. For instance, the input interface of the unlabelled hyperedge in\penalty\ \eqref{eq:exhierarchicalhyp} is the list consisting of two nodes, labeled $A$ and $B$ respectively, and the output interface is the list consisting of a single node labelled $B$.
\par\par\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\par The definition of hierarchical hypergraphs is agnostic on the set of objects labelling the nodes, as the only requirement is that they match the type of the morphisms labelling the hyperedges. However, in modelling higher-order computation, we want to restrict attention to those hierarchical hypergraphs where layers enforce scoping discipline. Roughly speaking, this means that, for instance, if a `bubble' receives inputs of type $A$, and the hyperedges inside it have ingoing nodes labeled with $A$, $B$, and outgoing nodes labeled with $C$, $E$, then the output of the bubble should be of type $B\multimap(C\otimes E)$. This scoping discipline leads to the notion of \emph{hypernet}.
\par\begin{definition}A hypernet is a open hierarchical hypergraph $(L,G,R,f_{L},f_{R})$, with $G=(N,E,v,l_{n},l^{\prime}_{e})$ such that
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@it is a monogamous open hypergraph when forgetting about the hierarchical structure.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@if $l^{\prime}_{e}(f)\not\eq\bot$, then $f$ has no children (it is not parent of any node nor hyperedge).
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@if $l_{e}(f)=\bot$, then the hyperedge $f$ is a well-typed abstraction. That is, there exists some $B\in\Sigma_{0}$ such that $f$ has $[A,B]$ as list of labels of nodes on the input interface, where $A$ is the label of the ingoing node of $f$, and the outgoing node from $f$ is labeled with $B\multimap C$, where $C$ is the list of labels of nodes on the output interface of $f$. \end{itemize}\end{definition}\par We are now in position to give a combinatorial interpretation of hierarchical string diagrams in terms of the structures we just introduced. { We take as starting point the SCMC $reelygeneratedbyaclosedmonoidalsignature$(\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1)$,asdescribedinDefinition\penalty\ \ref{def:freeSCMC}.Asdiscussedtherein,objectsofaSCMChaveamorecomplexstructurethanobjectsinaSMC.Therefore,toproperlyinterpretstringdiagramsin$we label nodes with arbitrary objects of $notjustthegeneratingones.Asfarasmorphismsareconcerned,weextendtheinterpretationofDefinition\penalty\ \ref{def:hypint}withclausesfollowingthefreeconstructionof$That means, we include two extra clauses, for evaluation and for abstraction, as follows.
