\end{figure}\par\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Further reading and related work}
\par For rewriting of string diagrams in symmetric monoidal categories, the most comprehensive reference is the series of works\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:journals/jacm/BonchiGKSZ22,BonchiGKSZ22b,BonchiGKSZ22c}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}, which details the correspondence with DPO rewriting of open hypergraphs. We refer to this source for all the details which we omitted in this survey chapter.
\par We mentioned how the variant that is both sound and complete for string diagram rewriting is \emph{convex} DPO-rewriting. We did not mention that, conversely, the standard notion of DPO-rewriting also has a natural string diagrammatic counterpart: it is sound and complete for so-called hypergraph categories, i.e. SMCs with a chosen Frobenius algebra structure on each object. Rewriting for string diagrams in categories with structure intermediate between symmetric monoidal and Frobenius has also been studied:\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2204-04274}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} gives a sound and complete DPO-rewriting interpretation for SMCs with a commutative monoid structure on each object, and\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{GhicaKayeTracedComonoid}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} does the same for traced comonoid structure. For the case of monoidal closed categories, and rewriting of hierarchical string diagrams, we refer to\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/fscd/Alvarez-Picallo22}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}. All these work crucially rest on the fact that pushouts in categories of (hyper)graphs are well-behaved, and adapted to DPO rewriting. These features have been studied on a case-by-case basis for a long time, see e.g.\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{Corradinietal-graphtransf}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}, and at a later stage encapsulated more abstractly in the notion of \emph{adhesive category}, in\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/fossacs/LackS04}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}. The various notions of hypergraphs we introduced all form adhesive categories. For hierarchical hypergraphs, proving this is not at all trivial; it has been worked out only recently, in\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/fossacs/CastelnovoGM22}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
\par Whereas the literature on rewriting in categories that are \emph{at least} symmetric monoidal is quite rich, far less is known on rewriting in categories without symmetries. The case of monoidal categories has only been investigated with a `native' approach, in which the laws of monoidal categories are considered as additional rewrite rules, rather than structural --- see in particular\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/ac/Lafont93,lafontpeaks}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}, and\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:journals/corr/Mimram14}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} for an overview on this approach. To the best of our knowledge, a graph interpretation for this class of string diagrams has not been studied yet, and the same is true for braided monoidal categories, which are intermediate between monoidal and symmetric monoidal.
\par Together with the theoretical developments, various tools have been proposed to perform diagrammatic reasoning, which exploit the correspondence with DPO rewriting in its implementation. {Quantomatic}\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{kissinger_quantomatic:_2015}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} is perhaps the earliest example, which assumes that string diagrams may be manipulated as if they were in a compact-closed category --- this assumption is stronger than symmetric monoidal, but (slightly) weaker than hypergraph categories. The more recent {Cartographer}\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/calco/SobocinskiWZ19}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} works instead at the level of generality of string diagrams in symmetric monoidal categories. Last we mention\penalty\ {Globular}\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{globular}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}, and the associated project\penalty\ {Homotopy.io}, which is intended as a visual aid for reasoning in higher categories; (symmetric) monoidal categories are a special case, which however is treated without absorbing any structural rules --- all the laws of the category are regarded as rewrite rules. The tool landscape for hypernets is relatively less mature, including only one tool of note, {SD Visualiser}, aimed at rendering and exploring large diagrams but with no rewriting support at the moment.
\par\par\lx@newpage\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{Operational Semantics of $\lambda$ Calculi}
\par Repeated applications of the $\beta$ rule may transform a term into another term where further $\beta$ reductions are impossible.
Such irreducible terms are sometimes called \emph{normal forms} or \emph{values}, depending of context.
The rewriting theory of the $\lambda$ calculus is \emph{confluent}, in the sense that the ultimate normal form, if any, is not sensitive to the order in which reductions are applied.
The study of confluence is a key concern of the theory of the $\lambda$ calculus, but we shall not pursue it here.
\par In contrast, when the $\lambda$ calculus is used as a \emph{programming language} the equations are not applied arbitrarily wherever possible, but according to a schedule, or \emph{evaluation strategy}.
Recall that a \emph{redex} is a sub-term that can be rewritten in a way that is consistent with the left-hand-side of an equation.
The \emph{evaluation strategy} is the way in which a term is repeatedly scanned for a redex, then rewritten according to the equation that matches the redex.
We call this step-by-step transformation of a term a \emph{reduction sequence}, and the system of rules that governs it an \emph{operational semantics}.
Operational semantics can be specified in several ways, but here we will give what is in some sense the simplest presentation, the so-called \emph{big-step} operational semantics.
\par Perhaps the most common evaluation strategy is the \emph{call-by-value} (CBV) strategy in which the argument of a function is evaluated before the function is applied.
To define it we first define the concept of \emph{value} as a syntactic form:
$$\mathcal{V}::=x\mid\lambda x.u.$$We use $w\in\mathcal{V}$ to range over values.
Evaluation of a term $u$ will stop if and only if it results in a value $w$,
written as $u\Downarrow_{v}w$.
\begin{definition}$$\frac{w\in\mathcal{V}}{w\Downarrow_{v}w}\qquad\frac{u\Downarrow_{v}\lambda x.u^{\prime}\quad v\Downarrow_{v}w\quad u^{\prime}[x/w]\Downarrow_{v}w^{\prime}}{u\,v\Downarrow_{v}w^{\prime}}.$$\end{definition}Contrast this with the \emph{call-by-name} $\lambda$ calculus in which the argument of a function is not evaluated at application:
\begin{definition}$$\frac{w\in\mathcal{V}}{w\Downarrow_{n}w}\qquad\frac{u\Downarrow_{n}\lambda x.u^{\prime}\quad u^{\prime}[x/v]\Downarrow_{v}w}{u\,v\Downarrow_{v}w}.$$\end{definition}This small change has vast repercussion over the behaviour of the $\lambda$ calculus used as a programming language, both in terms of time and space efficiency and equational properties.
These matters are beyond the scope of this tutorial.
\begin{example}\begin{center}\vskip 3.44444pt plus 3.44444pt minus 1.72218pt
\ignorespaces
\ignorespaces \ignorespaces

\ignorespaces\vskip 3.44444pt plus 3.44444pt minus 1.72218pt\end{center}The double line indicates that the terms involved in that relation are syntactically equal (up to $\alpha$ renaming), namely $x[x/\lambda y.y]=\lambda y.y$.
\end{example}\par The concept of \emph{confluence} mentioned earlier is reflected by the following property:
\begin{theorem}If $u$ is a closed term of STLC and $u\Downarrow_{v}w$, $u\Downarrow_{n}w^{\prime}$, then $w=w^{\prime}$.
\end{theorem}The proof is beyond the scope of this tutorial.
\par However, for untyped $\lambda$ calculi the confluence theorem does not hold.
\begin{example}Consider the term $\omega:=(\lambda x.xx)(\lambda y.yy)$ and its CBV evaluation:
\par\begin{center}\vskip 3.44444pt plus 3.44444pt minus 1.72218pt

\ignorespaces\vskip 3.44444pt plus 3.44444pt minus 1.72218pt\end{center}Note that the evaluation runs into some kind of a circular reference in which evaluating $\omega$ requires evaluating $\omega$ itself,
so the derivation tree cannot be finite.
Using the CBN strategy would run into the same problem.
\end{example}These kind of terms that cannot be evaluated are said to be \emph{divergent}.
\par\begin{exercise}CBV and CBN have distinct divergence properties.
Check that $(\lambda x.y)\omega\Downarrow_{n}y$ whereas there is no $w\in\mathcal{V}$ such that $(\lambda x.y)\omega\Downarrow_{v}w$.
\end{exercise}\par The big-step style of presenting the operational semantics obscures to some extent the computational processes involved in the evaluation.
This is particularly salient in the case of the divergent term in which we can only exhibit a partially constructed derivation tree.
This partial construction indicates implicitly that in our attempt to construct the tree we expand certain branches of the tree first, using the results to then expand other branches.
These computational processes are made more explicit in other styles of operational semantics, namely \emph{small-step} or \emph{abstract machine} operational semantics.
We will give an operational semantics using string diagrams which as we shall see makes the computational aspects completely explicit.
This style of semantics would allow a meaningful interpretation of divergent but useful programs, for example servers that endlessly wait for and handle connections.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{String diagrams and operational semantics for CBV}
The presentation of operational semantics will be given in the informal but rigorous style we prefer, noting that the formalisation as graph rewriting in the previous section remains valid.
\par We start by adding a \emph{decoration}, or a pointer, to a selected wire in a string diagram, which explicates the process of searching for a redex.
The left-pointing triangle indicates a part of the diagram which is about to be evaluated, whereas the right-pointing triangle points away from a part of the diagram that was just evaluated.
So the string diagram operational semantics will give rules for moving the pointer around in the diagram, plus the application of rewrites corresponding to the scheduled application of the particular equations:
\begin{definition}$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{opsem.pdf}}\put(0.53064,0.69371){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\beta}}{{\rightsquigarrow}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{opsem.pdf}}\put(0.53064,0.5105){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{C}{1}}}{{\rightsquigarrow}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.53064,0.27219){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{C}{2}}}{{\rightsquigarrow}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.53064,0.07105){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\stackrel{{\scriptstyle V}}{{\rightsquigarrow}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.53064,1.02906){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{S}{1}}}{{\rightsquigarrow}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.53064,0.91036){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{S}{2}}}{{\rightsquigarrow}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{opsem.pdf}}\end{picture}$$Initially the diagram is annotated with a left-pointing triangle on the rightmost wire.
The evaluation succeeds if a right-pointing triangle is present on the rightmost-wire.
\end{definition}The rules can be read informally as follows:
\begin{description}\description@item@[Structural rule 1 (S1)]To evaluate an application, first evaluate the function.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\description@item@[Structural rule 2 (S2)]After evaluating a function, evaluate the argument.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\description@item@[Beta rule ($\beta$))]After evaluating the argument apply the $\beta$ and evaluate the result.
Note the rule here uses a more economical version of $\beta$ in which the argument is not actually involved.
It is rather similar to the cancellation of the evaluation and co-evaluation in the adjunction.
Also note the change of direction in the pointer, to re-evaluate the result of this rule.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\description@item@[Copying 1 (C1)]When encountering a copy node copy the node it connects to, in effect using the naturality of the Cartesian product.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\description@item@[Copying 2 (C2)]Just like the above, but from the other side of the copying node.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\description@item@[Value (V)]An abstraction is a value.
Note the change of direction in the pointer.
\end{description}\par\begin{remark}Something that is remarkable but easy to overlook is that the transition rules in Definition\penalty\ \ref{def:cbvsd} are \emph{small}, i.e. they only involve local rewrites of the string diagram.
This is obviously the case for the $\beta$ rule in which substitution is not really invoked, but rather essentially consists only of a cancellation of the evaluation/co-evaluation pair of adjunctions.
The actual substitution is effected by the evaluation pointer reaching copy nodes, which trigger the replication of diagrams but in a controlled, stepwise fashion.
This is a clearer execution model in terms of understanding the time and space costs involved in the evaluation, compared to relying on the meta-syntactic use of substitution.
Also local are the structural rules, which show the way the evaluation pointer interacts with the evaluation operation independent of its arguments.
\end{remark}\par\begin{example}In Figure\penalty\ \ref{fig:exopsem} we reprise Example\penalty\ \ref{ex:idid3} in the diagrammatic formulation.
The dummy transitions labelled with $=$ are just re-drawings of the diagram, to emphasise a redex or just to tidy up.

However, this hyperedge should not be considered a `box' in the language of string diagrams, i.e. a morphism (or a family of morphisms) in the category, because it is not part of the language syntax.
Certain diagrammatic equations involving the pointer should hold, for instance
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ptrnotsd.pdf}}\put(0.4158,0.17956){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{ptrnotsd.pdf}}\end{picture}$$However, such diagrams are ill formed, illegal configurations.
This is not problematic beyond the obvious consequence that the strategic aspects of the operational semantics are not given a categorical interpretation.
\end{remark}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsubsection}{toc}{Calculi of explicit substitutions}
Substitution plays a critical role in the syntax and equational theory of the $\lambda$ calculus.
At the same time substitution is a \emph{meta-syntactic} construct, which is makes formalisation more difficult, especially when it comes to understanding the computational cost of substitution.
The substitution rules in particular as a meta-operation can have a widely varying and complex cost involving the identification of variables, $\alpha$-renamings, and copying of terms of various sizes.
\par Calculi of explicit substitution (ES) deal with this problem by making substitution a term former in the language, so that
$$u::=x\mid u\,u\mid\lambda x.u\mid u[x/u].$$This formulation may raise some subtle syntactic issue regarding scope, binding, and alpha equivalence which are either swept under the carpet as bureaucratic annoyances or resolved by using DeBruijn indices instead of variable names.
The latter makes syntax easier to formalise, but the downside of using indices is, of course, that the syntax becomes utterly unreadable.
\par The rules of substitution are made into explicit language equations:
\begin{definition}Assuming $x\neq y$,
\@@amsalign
\end{definition}\par With the exception of the last equation, all the above are directed (left-to-right) and can immediately form the basis of a rewrite system.
The last equation (dubbed the $C$-rule) is problematic computationally because it is undirected, so it has the same status as the $\alpha$ rule.
Indeed, equivalence of terms is up to these two equations ($\alpha$ and $C$).
\par We have seen that one of the key advantages of the string diagram notation is that it absorbs certain equations into isomorphic graphs.
This is also the case for the $C$-rule; using the interpretation of substitution (Lemma\penalty\ \ref{lem:subst}) we can see that the left-hand side, $\bigl(u[x/v]\bigr)[x^{\prime}/v^{\prime}]$ is, after cancelling out some copy-discard pairs, isomorphic to the graph below, which is in turn isomorphic to the right-hand side.

the correctness of ES equations in the string diagram interpretation.
\end{exercise}\begin{remark}The significant notational simplification introduced by the use of string diagrams in the calculus of explicit substitutions does not come at the expense of informality.
It is true that the \emph{presentation} here is informal, for pedagogical reasons, but the formally minded reader has already seen how string diagrams can be presented as precisely defined combinatorial structures.
Eliminating not one, but two quotient rules from the formal representation of the calculus is a significant notational advantage.
\end{remark}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Applied $\lambda$ calculi}
\par The $\lambda$ calculus provides the infrastructure upon which programming languages are built.
Function calls represent the ``mortar'' that binds together the software ``bricks'' that constitute a program: the operations.
Enhancing the $\lambda$ calculus with operations leads to an \emph{applied} $\lambda$ calculus, an idealised programming language.
Practical programming languages represent the final elaboration, with numerous and complex operations and a more sophisticated syntax.
Let us review several common such operations, their defining equations, and their operational semantics.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsubsection}{toc}{Arithmetic and logic}
\par\par Here and henceforth we shall treat matters of superficial syntax with a certain degree of informality which should not cause confusion.
Whenever convenient we use human-readable syntax common in most languages (e.g. $1+2$) but when we want to avoid ambiguities we will switch to a de-sugared notation (e.g. $\mathit{add}\,(1,2)$) or a categorical representation (e.g. $(1\otimes 2)\mathbin{;}\mathit{add}$).
\par\par Adding arithmetic and logic requires:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@one (or more) numerical type $\mathit{Num}$ (e.g. $\mathit{Float}$ or $\mathit{Int}$ or $\mathit{Bool}$),
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@numerical constants $m,n,p,\ldots:I\to\mathit{Num}$ (e.g. $7:I\to\mathit{Int}$ or $4.5:I\to\mathit{Float}$),
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@unary operators $\mathit{op}:\mathit{Num}\to\mathit{Num}$ (e.g. $\mathit{neg}:\mathit{Int}\to\mathit{Int}$),
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@arithmetic operators $\mathit{op}:\mathit{Num}\times\mathit{Num}\to\mathit{Num}$ (e.g. $\mathit{add}:\mathit{Int}\times\mathit{Int}\to\mathit{Int}$),
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@logical operators $\mathit{op}:\mathit{Num}\times\mathit{Num}\to\mathit{Bool}$ (e.g. $\mathit{less\_than}:\mathit{Int}\times\mathit{Int}\to\mathit{Bool}$),
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@conversion operations $\mathit{conv}:\mathit{Num}\to\mathit{Num}^{\prime}$ (e.g. $\mathit{floor}:\mathit{Float}\to\mathit{Int}$), etc.
\end{itemize}\par The equations governing these operations are the obvious ones, and they are obviously directed (e.g. $1+1=2$) so they form a natural basis for an operational semantics.
For binary operations, the structural rules $S1$ and $S2$ in Definition\penalty\ \ref{def:cbvsd}, which give the order of evaluation (right-to-left) can be reused.
The value rule $V$ in the same Definition can also be reused, as numerical constants are values and require no further evaluation.
Finally, each operation has an associated reduction rule (sometimes called a $\delta$ rule):

is obvious that each $\delta$ rule, which always produce a value, can be immediately combined with the value rule $V$ to give the composite rule
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{vdelta.pdf}}\put(0.02506,0.19307){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$m$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.03079,0.06419){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$n$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.63222,0.12577){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$p$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{vdelta.pdf}}\put(0.20119,0.12863){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{op}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.59642,0.00691){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$p=\mathit{op}(m,n)$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.41866,0.12729){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$We decline to perform this `optimisation' for the sake of keeping uniform the interaction between structural rules, which show how the pointer traverses the graph without changing it, with the rewrite rules which update the graph.
Namely, a rewrite rule will always produce a pointer aiming to the left, back into the recently produced term, as rewrites do not generally produce values as results (e.g. $\beta$ reduction).
\end{remark}The following is left to the reader.
\begin{exercise}Define appropriate string-diagram operational semantics for unary and conversion operators.
\end{exercise}\par\@@numbered@section{subsubsection}{toc}{If-then-else and other shortcut operators}
\par\par A naive if-then-else operator can be defined as $\mathit{ite}:\mathit{Bool}\times\mathit{Num}\times\mathit{Num}\to\mathit{Num}$, with equations
\@@amsgather
But this does not give enough hints as to how the if-then-else operator is to be evaluated.
An obvious extension of the structural rules $S1$ and $S2$ to rules for ternary operators is not good enough, because it would give the following undesired equalities, where $\omega$ is any diverging term:
\@@amsgather
thus violating our intended equations for the special case of $\omega$.
\par There is one way the evaluation of the arguments after that of test expression can be prevented, which is the same way the evaluation of bodies of functions is prevented: thunking them.
The thunks of the branches of an if-then-else statement take no arguments, so they are of the shape $\Lambda_{I}(u)$.
Thus, an if-then-else statement written as $\mathit{if\ b\ then\ u\ else\ v}$ in the surface language is interpreted as
$$\mathit{ite}(b,\Lambda_{I}(t),\Lambda_{I}(u)),$$noting that our problematic evaluations are not so anymore, with $\Lambda_{I}(\omega)$ being a value rather than a divergent computation.
So the two equations are:
\@@amsgather
With this interpretation in place, structural rules $S1$ and $S2$, along with an obvious new rule $S3$, can be extended to handle ternary operators.
The $V$ rule for thunks is still used as before, to prevent the evaluation of $t$ and $u$.
The sole genuine extension are the two reduction rules for the if-then-else, shown in their graphical form, and involving both a selection of the thunk and its `forcing':

For instance, in the rewrite of the if-then-else operation potentially large sub-graphs `disappear'.
The reader is left to compare, in terms of possible cost model (time and space) the rules given above with rules which create inaccessible, from the point of view of evaluation, sub-graphs, usually called \emph{garbage} (only one of the rules shown):

\end{exercise}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsubsection}{toc}{Recursion}
\par It is straightforward to include a standard recursion operator, with the rule
$$\mathit{rec}(\lambda f.u)=u\bigr[f/\mathit{rec}(\lambda f.u)\bigl]$$noting that this is an ``expansion'' rather than a ``reduction'' rule.
\par The recursion operator has a single argument, which is a thunk so it will use the unary version of the structural rule along with the rewrite:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rec.pdf}}\put(0.08048,0.03448){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rec.pdf}}\put(0.22978,0.03766){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{rec}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rec.pdf}}\put(0.6364,0.03448){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rec.pdf}}\put(0.90642,0.03448){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{rec.pdf}}\put(0.73646,0.03614){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{rec}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.39174,0.03667){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$\par\begin{remark}The reader acquainted more casually with programming languages with recursion may feel slightly confused by the use of recursion as an operator, rather than as a binding construct.
But the conventional recursive binding found in common programming languages can be easily \emph{interpreted} with the help of a recursion operator.
A definition such as
$$f(x)=\cdots f(\cdots x\cdots)\cdots$$is interpreted as
$$\mathit{rec}(\lambda f\lambda x.\cdots f(\cdots x\cdots)\cdots)$$\end{remark}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsubsection}{toc}{Abortive continuations}
\par Prior to recursion, all operations we consider had ``reductive'' rules in which the result is smaller, as a graph, than the operands.
A graph could still grow because of copying, but not because of the application of an operation.
Recursion, in contrast, expands the graph via the application of an operation.
\par However, something that all operations to this point share is that the result of their application does not create new thunks.
But now we will see just this, a thunk-creating operation called ``\emph{call/cc}''.
This operation is a very powerful control operator that can be used to implement a wide range of simpler and more common control operations, such as exceptions.
To be effective it works in tandem with another operation, \emph{abort}.
\par Another distinction between the \emph{call/cc} rules and the rules seen so far is that the previous rules are ``small'' in the sense that they only involve a part of the graph that is situated to the left of the pointer, whereas the \emph{call/cc} rules involve not only the operands, but also the \emph{context} in which the operation is executed.
\par The rules are as below:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.09594,0.06323){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.19866,0.06568){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{call{/}cc}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.34697,0.06633){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$t$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.09288,0.17328){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.20538,0.17573){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{abort}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.53309,0.17328){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.34392,0.17639){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$t$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.70979,0.02899){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{abort}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.85408,0.03878){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.62822,0.02965){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$t$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.94615,0.05411){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$t$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{callcc.pdf}}\put(0.43021,0.1754){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.43021,0.06734){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$\par The rules are global, in the sense that the sub-graph $t$, in both rules, is such that its root is the overall root of the graph.
Such global rules are sometimes called \emph{program reductions}, in contrast with the more common, local, \emph{term reductions} seen earlier.
The sub-graph term is usually called \emph{the context} of the evaluation and both rules manipulate it.
The \emph{abort} rule is so called because it ``aborts'' its execution context $t$ and performs is argument instead.
The \emph{call/cc} rule makes the context into a so-called ``abortive continuation'' creating a thunk in which the context $t$ is ``guarded'' by an \emph{abort} operation.
Whenever this thunk is executed, the abort will cause the context at the time to be discarded and perform the continuation instead.
\par\begin{remark}Other control operations such as exceptions, delimited continuations, or effect handlers can be implemented in a similar style.
These are left as an exercise.
\end{remark}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsubsection}{toc}{Store}
\par A common feature of programming languages is \emph{store}, also known as \emph{mutable variables} (variables which actually vary).
One of the earliest systematic attempts at a language with higher order functions and store is {Algol60}.
The extensions consist of a new type $Var$ for mutable variables along with the following operations
\@@amsalign
\begin{example}A term that in some conventional concrete syntax would be written as
\begin{verbatim}
var x ; x = x + 1
\end{verbatim}
would be desugared as
$$\mathit{newvar}(\lambda x.\mathit{assign}\ x\ (add\ (\mathit{deref}\ x)\ 1))$$\end{example}The configuration of the term reduction semantics, which has shape $t\to t^{\prime}$, is expanded with an additional component $s$, a partial function $\mathcal{L}\rightharpoonup\mathcal{V}$ where $\mathcal{L}$ is a set of \emph{locations} (also known as \emph{references} or \emph{atoms}) and $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of values.
\par Describing the behaviour of store equationally is possible but too complicated to delve into here and also rather unusual.
The standard approach is to use \emph{operational semantics}, a reduction semantics in which configurations consists of terms and \emph{stores}, i.e. partial maps from a new data type of \emph{locations} (or \emph{references}) and values, $s:\mathcal{L}\rightharpoonup\mathcal{V}$.
\par We will first give a string diagram semantics which is an instance of what we have seen so far, then enhance it for readability with additional graphical conventions.
\par The rule for new variable declaration is
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{store.pdf}}\put(0.26326,0.07709){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{newvar}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{store.pdf}}\put(0.1229,0.07474){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{store.pdf}}\put(0.88201,0.09239){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{store.pdf}}\put(0.63486,0.02177){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$a$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{store.pdf}}\put(0.75844,0.07473){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mapsto$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{store.pdf}}\put(0.63486,0.1277){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{store.pdf}}\put(0.48927,0.07516){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$where $a$ is \emph{fresh}, i.e. it is not used anywhere in the diagram and $v_{0}$ is a default initial value.
\begin{remark}The choice of $a$ is irrelevant, so long as it is some fresh value.
No program construct can distinguish between two distinct choices of atoms $a\neq a^{\prime}$, a property known as \emph{equivariance}.
The data structure of locations is extremely simple, for which reason its elements are called \emph{atoms}.
In this conceptual \emph{API} there are only two operations: creating fresh atoms and testing two atoms for equality.
This data structure has been extensively studied within the framework of \emph{nominal sets}.
Equivariance is an essential property of more complex structures containing such atoms.
\end{remark}The rule for dereferencing is obvious, extracting the value $v$ associated with the dereferencing location $a$:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{deref.pdf}}\put(0.02707,0.02862){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$a$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{deref.pdf}}\put(0.18948,0.09822){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mapsto$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{deref.pdf}}\put(0.02707,0.16783){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{deref.pdf}}\put(0.86234,0.09822){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{deref.pdf}}\put(0.37395,0.10132){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{deref}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.66487,0.10403){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$The rule for assignment is more unusual because, as in the case of control, it is \emph{non-local} relative to the structure of the overall diagram:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.33925,0.36403){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{assign}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.02092,0.25523){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$a$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.14645,0.30903){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mapsto$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.02092,0.36283){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.02092,0.47042){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v^{\prime}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.72027,0.36283){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v_{0}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.2899,0.02212){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$a$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.41543,0.07591){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mapsto$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.2899,0.12971){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.72027,0.02212){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$a$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.8458,0.07591){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mapsto$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.72027,0.12971){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v^{\prime}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{asg.pdf}}\put(0.57399,0.08378){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.56565,0.36855){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$The first rule states that evaluating the assignment operation returns a default value, not necessarily the same as the default initialisation value (in most languages it is the unique inhabitant of the singleton type).
\par The second rule states that \emph{every subgraph} in which $v$ is associated with $a$ is rewritten so that $v$ is replaced by $v^{\prime}$.
As given, the rule is correct in terms of input-output behaviour of a programming language with store, but extremely inefficient.
Every assignment requires searching for the relevant location $a$ in the diagram so that its corresponding value can be updated.
\par We can improve our graphical notation with the following convention: identify all nodes labelled by the same atom $a$ in the diagram, i.e keep all the occurrences of the subgraph mapping the same $a$ to $v$ shared via contraction.
This is possible because the category is still Cartesian and because it is an invariant of the diagram that the same $a$ is always mapped to the same $v$.
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.47792,0.2097){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.36999,0.20842){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$t$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.02376,0.26952){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$a$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.16633,0.33062){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mapsto$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.02376,0.39172){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.02376,0.02512){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$a$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.16633,0.08622){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mapsto$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.02376,0.14732){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.89952,0.20842){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$t$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.57366,0.14732){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$a$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.71623,0.20842){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mapsto$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\put(0.57366,0.26952){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{atom1.pdf}}\end{picture}$$Since the identity of the atom $a$ is irrelevant due to equivariance we can elide it, as we can elide the $\mapsto$ operation.
What we are left with is:

\end{example}\par\begin{remark}The streamlined rule for assignment and dereferencing may seem not to apply, and consequently require a special case, when the atom is only reachable via a single edge in the diagram.
In this situation the graph can be rewritten, using the properties of copy and discard to an equal graph which fits the required format, so it can be reduced:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{garbage.pdf}}\put(0.32759,0.10062){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{deref}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{garbage.pdf}}\put(0.04416,0.02842){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{garbage.pdf}}\put(0.80453,0.02842){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{garbage.pdf}}\put(0.80453,0.14362){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{garbage.pdf}}\put(0.30455,0.35408){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}${\mathit{deref}}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{garbage.pdf}}\put(0.02688,0.351){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{garbage.pdf}}\put(0.77835,0.36025){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$???$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.29608,0.23272){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.61956,0.3621){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.6165,0.08346){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\end{picture}$$Also using the properties of copy and discard the subgraph linked to the discard node, consisting of the atom and an occurrence of $v$ can be entirely removed.
From an operational perspective this quiet automatic removal of a reference and its contents whenever it is unreachable from the main graph is an abstract counterpart of the so-called \emph{garbage collection} performed by runtime systems of programming languages with managed memory.
\end{remark}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Further reading and related work}
The material presented here is mostly based on the graph rewriting abstract machines of \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:journals/lmcs/MuroyaG19}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} and \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1907-01257}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
An online interactive tool can help explore the step-by-step reduction of programs with many of the features discussed in this section.
For the wider context of operational semantics there are many introductory tutorials, from the concise \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/ac/Pitts00}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} to the extensive \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{harper16}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
The world of abstract machines in programming languages is also extensive and diverse, with an extensive annotated bibliography given in \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:journals/fgcs/DiehlHS00a}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
The connection between operational semantics and abstract machines is quite technical, especially when the latter is meant to be extracted from the former, rather than proven \emph{post facto} as a correct implementation; a collection of such extractions is given in \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/icfp/AccattoliBM14}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
\par We have only touched onto the issue of strategic graph rewriting, and in a naive way. More sophisticated approaches to strategic graph rewriting have been studied in the context of graph-oriented programming languages\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/lopstr/FernandezKN11}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
\par The calculus of explicit substitutions was introduced by \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:journals/jfp/AbadiCCL91}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} and it spawned a large literature.
Of particular relevance are the connections with graph representations via proof nets \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:journals/tcs/Accattoli15}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} and interaction nets \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/tlca/Sinot05}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
\par\par\par\lx@newpage\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{Case Studies}
\par String diagrams are a data structure for the representation of syntax with higher-order bindings.
The best motivation for a new data structure are the algorithms it can enable and support.
Case in point, we will consider three well-known such classes of algorithms: type inference, closure conversion, and reverse automatic differentiation.
We choose these algorithms because in their original, term-based formulation they can be rather mysterious to the average compiler developer, who may struggle to tease out the intuition from what is usually a complex syntactic analysis or transformation.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Type inference}
\par Type inference is the process of determining whether a term in which the variables have not been assigned a type can be assigned a type.
To give a trivial example, the term $x+1$ can be successfully assigned an integer type, which makes the term correctly typed presuming that 1 is itself an integer and addition requires two integer parameters. A type inference algorithm in this case will determine first that it is possible to assign a type to the variable and, if needed, produce that type.
As a consequence, the variable $x$ occurring in the term will also be required to have an integer type.
\par On the contrary, in the term $\mathit{if}\ x\ \mathit{then}\ x+1\ \mathit{else}\ 0$ it is not possible to assign a type to $x$ since the if statement demands it be a Boolean, whereas addition requires it to be an integer.
Both these constraints cannot be satisfied simultaneously in a simple type system.
\par As we can glean from these very simple examples, a type inference algorithms must perform three kinds of computations:
\begin{enumerate}\enumerate@item@build a system of constraints determined by the syntactic structure of the term and the known types of operations or constants occurring in the term;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@check whether the system is consistent, i.e. there are no constraints that are not solvable;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@determine the missing types of variables if required.
\end{enumerate}The first step is usually computationally cheap, requiring a single pass over the term.
The second step can be computationally expensive, asymptotically exponential time for a typical algorithm, although this worst case scenario is highly contrived.
However, the potentially high complexity of the algorithm indicates that there is plenty of room for optimising heuristics that can make a difference in practice.
And indeed this is where various type inference algorithms can take different approaches.
Another source of significant optimisation is only computing the precise types of variables that need to be computed, avoiding potentially expensive type determinations if they are not strictly required.
\par In this expository presentation of type inference using string diagrams we will not commit to any particular algorithm but we shall expose the essence of type inference so that it should be rather obvious how various heuristic choices can lead to various concrete algorithms.
\par The first important idea is that when representing syntax as string diagrams type inference becomes an \emph{edge-labelling problem}.
To stay focussed we will illustrate this algorithm for the concrete case of (unrecursive) PCF, i.e. $\lambda$ calculus plus if-then-else, and arithmetic-logic operators.
The language of types is given by the grammar
$$T::=\mathit{Bool}\mid\mathit{Int}\mid T\rightarrow T\mid\alpha$$i.e. Booleans, natural numbers, function types, and unknown or indeterminate types.
Concrete variables for indeterminate types are written as (decorated) Greek alphabet letters.
\par\par Before talking about type inference we need to briefly introduce the concept of \emph{unification}, which is the system of syntactic constraints that needs to be solved during inference.
Generally speaking, unification is an algorithm that determines whether the variables of two expressions can be instantiated so that the expressions are equal.
The theory of unification is out of the scope of this tutorial so we will rely on naive intuitions, which hold for this simple language of types.
\par Let $\Gamma$ be an \emph{environment} mapping type variables to types.
\begin{enumerate}\enumerate@item@$\mathit{Int}$ and $\mathit{Int}$ unify in any environment;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@$\mathit{Bool}$ and $\mathit{Bool}$ unify in any environment;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@$\alpha$ and $T$ unify if $\alpha$ does not occur in $T$, in any environment in which $\alpha$ is instantiated to $T$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@$T_{1}\to T_{2}$ and $T_{1}^{\prime}\to T_{2}^{\prime}$ unify in an environment if $T_{i}$ and $T_{i}^{\prime}$ unify in that environment;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@if none of the rules apply the types cannot be unified.
\end{enumerate}For instance, in this given grammar of types:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@$\alpha$ and $\mathit{Bool}$ can be trivially unified whenever $\alpha$ is instantiated as $\mathit{Bool}$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$\alpha\to\mathit{Bool}$ and $\mathit{Int}\to\beta$ can be unified whenever $\alpha$ and $\mathit{Int}$ unify and so do $\beta$ and $\mathit{Bool}$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$\mathit{Int}$ and $\mathit{Bool}$ cannot be unified;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$\mathit{Int}\to\alpha$ and $\mathit{Bool}\to\beta$ cannot be unified;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@$\alpha\to\beta$ and $\alpha$ cannot be unified.
\end{itemize}\par The syntax of terms is
$$t::=n\mid\mathit{tt}\mid\mathit{ff}\mid x\mid op\mid\mathit{if}\ t\ \mathit{then}\ t\ \mathit{else}\ t\mid t(t)\mid\lambda x.t$$that is, integer constants, boolean constants, variables, arithmetic-logic operators, if-then-else, function application and function abstraction.
\par The abstract algorithm, i.e. without committing to any particular heuristics, can be expressed as the construction of an \emph{unification graph} out of the term graph.
The emphasis will be on simplicity and clarity: a concrete, practical algorithm will require further optimisations and heuristics.
\par The initial unification graph has vertices $T$, the types, and edges $E=\emptyset$.
Even though the set of vertices is infinite, the set of edges will always remain finite, and we can safely ignore vertices which do not participate in any edge in $E$.
\par The algorithm consists of adding new edges to the unification graph, corresponding to each edge of the diagram representing the term.
We say that the outermost boxes are at \emph{level 0}, and the boxes contained by level-$n$ boxes are at level $n+1$.
Intuitively, the algorithm adds a \emph{decoration} to each wire, depending on the type, which can be either known (e.g. $\mathit{Int}$ for arithmetic operations) or unknown (case in which a fresh type variable is used) or partially known (the case of functions).
\par\par\lx@algorithmicx@beginlist@{}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 0.0pt{procedure}\ {unify}($t$) \lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt$n\leftarrow$ highest level of $t$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{for}\ $i\leftarrow n$ down to $0$\ {do}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 30.6665pt{for}\ $b\leftarrow$ boxes at level $i$\ {do}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 45.99976pt{if}\ $b$ is constant $k$\ {then}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$e\leftarrow$ unique wire of $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt{decorate}($e,\mathit{Int}$)
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 45.99976pt{else}\ {if}\ $b$ is constant $\mathit{tt,ff}$\ {then}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$e\leftarrow$ unique wire of $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt{decorate}($e,\mathit{Bool}$)
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 45.99976pt{else}\ {if}\ $b$ is $\mathit{add}$\ {then} \lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$(e_{0},e_{1},e_{2})\leftarrow$ wires of $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt{for }{$j\leftarrow 0,2$}{ do } {decorate}($e_{j},\mathit{Int}$)
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 45.99976pt{else}\ {if}\ $b$ is {application}\ {then}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$e_{0}\leftarrow$ argument wire of $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$\alpha_{0}\leftarrow$ new fresh variable
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt{decorate}($e_{0},\alpha_{0}$)
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$e_{1}\leftarrow$ result wire of $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$\alpha_{1}\leftarrow$ new fresh variable
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt{decorate}($e_{1},\alpha_{1}$)
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$e_{2}\leftarrow$ function wire of $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt{decorate}($e_{2},\alpha_{0}\to\alpha_{1}$)
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 45.99976pt{else}\ {if}\ $b$ is {abstraction box}\ {then}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$e\leftarrow$ result wire of $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$\alpha_{0}\leftarrow$ type of bound wire inside $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$\alpha_{1}\leftarrow$ type of root of diagram inside $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt{decorate}($e,\alpha_{0}\to\alpha_{1}$)
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 45.99976pt{else}\ {if}\ $b$ is {contraction}\ {then}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$(e_{0},e_{1},e_{2})\leftarrow$ wires of $b$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt$\alpha\leftarrow$ new fresh variable
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 61.33301pt{for }{$j\leftarrow 0,2$}{ do } {decorate}($e_{j},\alpha$)
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 45.99976pt{end}\ {if}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 30.6665pt{end}\ {for}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{end}\ {for}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 0.0pt{end}\ {procedure}\lx@algorithmicx@endlist
\par Type information is extracted from the constants (Lines 5 and 8) and from arithmetic and logical operations (only addition is given on Line 11, all other operations are similar).
The operation of abstraction however is \emph{polymorphic} in the sense that it may involve arguments of different types at different points in the program, so it will only introduce a constraint between the type of the two arguments and that of its result.
Proceeding from the inner boxes outwards ensures that when we encounter an abstraction (Line 23) it has already been annotated at the interface with all type information, so the type information extracted from an abstraction may contain unknown types.
Contraction, which corresponds to variables in the syntax, introduces only unknown type variables, which must be the same along all wires.
\par\par New edges are added to the unification graph using the procedure below.
Decorations are a partial function $D$ from edges to types.
\lx@algorithmicx@beginlist@{}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 0.0pt{procedure}\ {decorate}($e,T$)\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{if}\ $D(e)$ is not defined\ {then}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 30.6665pt$D\leftarrow(D\mid e\mapsto T)$ \lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{else}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 30.6665pt$T^{\prime}\leftarrow D(e)$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 30.6665pt$E\leftarrow E\cup(T,T^{\prime})$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{end}\ {if}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 0.0pt{end}\ {procedure}\lx@algorithmicx@endlist
If an edge $e$ is not already annotated we add the type $T$ as an annotation.
If an edge is already annotated we retrieve the existing annotation $T^{\prime}$ and we add a new edge $(T,T^{\prime})$ to the edge set $E$ of the unification graph.
Note that because of how string diagrams are constructed it is impossible for a wire to receive more than two labels.
\par This concludes the first part of the algorithm, the construction of the unification graph, in time linear in the size of the original diagram.
\par\begin{example}Consider the unification graph produced by applying the algorithm above to the diagram of the term $\mathit{if}\ x\ \mathit{then}\ x+1\ \mathit{else}\ 0$.
The algorithm visits each interface wire once and each other wire exactly twice, so we decorate each wire with the corresponding types.
In Figure\penalty\ \ref{fig:unifgraph} we show the edge-decorated diagram and the resulting unification graph.
\end{example}\par\begin{figure}$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph.pdf}}\put(0.56042,0.12932){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}{Unify}\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.41686,0.10863){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{if}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph.pdf}}\put(0.22269,0.10766){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.12164,0.16174){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$1$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.20944,0.26505){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$0$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.30108,0.2245){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$N,\alpha_{0}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.28062,0.12667){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$N,\alpha_{0}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.07223,0.01013){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{1},B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(-0.00019,0.07386){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{1}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.47426,0.1268){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{0}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0954,0.06807){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{1},N$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.17362,0.18394){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$N,N$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph.pdf}}\put(0.86885,0.16946){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{1}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph.pdf}}\put(0.73898,0.16962){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{0}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph.pdf}}\put(0.76218,0.03136){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$N$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph.pdf}}\put(0.89222,0.03184){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph.pdf}}\end{picture}$$\@@toccaption{{\lx@tag[ ]{{17}}{Example term and its unification graph}}}\@@caption{{\lx@tag[: ]{{\small Figure 17}}{\small Example term and its unification graph}}}
\end{figure}\par The second part of the algorithm is the computationally intensive part: checking whether an unification graph is valid.
The example above already discloses the validation condition: \emph{there should be no path from $\mathit{Int}$ to $\mathit{Bool}$ in the unification graph}.
Note that the failure of this condition can be determined without solving all the unknown type assignments of the term.
However, the solution is not always so straightforward when function types are involved.
\begin{example}Consider the unification graph produced by applying the algorithm above to the diagram of the term $f(\mathit{tt})+f(1)$.
Figure\penalty\ \ref{fig:unifgraph2} shows the edge-decorated diagram and the resulting unification graph.
\end{example}\par\begin{figure}$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.43535,0.11471){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}{Unify}\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.3515,0.09887){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$+$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.16328,0.09605){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$1$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.16296,0.18219){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{tt}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.60878,0.11668){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{1}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.53495,0.11668){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{0}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.75644,0.11668){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{3}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.68261,0.11668){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{2}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.9041,0.11668){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{5}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.83027,0.11668){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{4}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.69172,0.00299){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{Int}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.76563,0.00299){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{Bool}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.57523,0.21357){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{1}\to\alpha_{2}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.79739,0.21411){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{4}\to\alpha_{5}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\put(0.38428,0.11069){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{0}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.27662,0.04708){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{2},\mathit{Int}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.05565,0.05955){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{3},\alpha_{1}\to\alpha_{2}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.05321,0.14356){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{3},\alpha_{4}\to\alpha_{5}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.27835,0.15447){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{5},\mathit{Int}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.19559,0.19577){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{Bool},\alpha_{4}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.19525,0.10896){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\mathit{Int},\alpha_{1}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph2.pdf}}\end{picture}$$\@@toccaption{{\lx@tag[ ]{{18}}{Example term and its unification graph}}}\@@caption{{\lx@tag[: ]{{\small Figure 18}}{\small Example term and its unification graph}}}
\end{figure}\par Note that in Example\penalty\ \ref{ex:unifgraph2} (Figure \ref{fig:unifgraph2}) the graph is disconnected, which means that there is not enough information to relate $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{4},\alpha_{5}$.
This is dealt with by the following algorithm.
\par\lx@algorithmicx@beginlist@{}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 0.0pt{procedure}\ {saturate}($E$)\lx@algorithmicx@hfill$\triangleright$ infer new edges in the unification graph
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325ptfind new path $(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{k})$ in $E$ such that
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt$v_{1}=t_{1}\to t_{2}$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt$v_{k}=t_{3}\to t_{4}$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{if}\ fail\ {then}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 30.6665ptresult $\leftarrow E$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{else}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 30.6665pt{saturate}($E\cup(t_{1},t_{3})\cup(t_{2},t_{4})$)
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{end}\ {if}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 0.0pt{end}\ {procedure}\lx@algorithmicx@endlist
\par As applied to Example\penalty\ \ref{ex:unifgraph2} the graph, the resulting graph is:
\par$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(0.13213,0.2406){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{1}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(-0.00264,0.2406){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{0}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(0.45408,0.2406){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{3}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(0.27563,0.2406){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{2}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(0.80225,0.2406){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{5}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(0.65,0.2406){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{4}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(0.32063,0.00616){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$N$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(0.47302,0.00616){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$B$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(0.08041,0.44041){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{1}\to\alpha_{2}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\put(0.53852,0.44151){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\alpha_{4}\to\alpha_{5}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{unifgraph3.pdf}}\end{picture}$$\par Old edges are grey, new saturation edges are solid black.
We can now detect an invalid path $\mathit{Int},\alpha_{1},\alpha_{4},\mathit{Bool}$ corresponding to a type error.
Besides this one, there is another validation condition that must be checked:
\par\lx@algorithmicx@beginlist@{}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 0.0pt{procedure}\ {validate}($E$)\lx@algorithmicx@hfill$\triangleright$ find type errors
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325ptfind path $(\mathit{Int},v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,\mathit{Bool})$ in $E$
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325ptfind path $(\alpha,v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,\alpha\to t)$ in $E$ or
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325ptfind path $(\alpha,v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,t\to\alpha)$ in $E$ or
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{if}\ fail\ {then}
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 30.6665ptresult $\leftarrow$ type ok
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{else}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 30.6665ptresult $\leftarrow$ type error
\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 15.33325pt{end}\ {if}\lx@algorithmicx@@item\noindent\hskip 0.0pt{end}\ {procedure}\lx@algorithmicx@endlist
\par The paths from a type variable to a type containing that variable arise from terms such as illegal self-application.
It is a simple exercise to check that $f\ f$, an impossible term in PCF, leads to a violation of this condition.
\par The {saturate} procedure is applied until it produces no new edges in the saturation graph.
Finding saturating paths is computationally intensive and this is where heuristics come into play.
In particular, it is not always necessary to add all saturating paths.
Also, saturation and validity checking can be cleverly interleaved to lead to earlier error detection.
\par\begin{exercise}Determine whether the following term type checks:
$$f(0)+g(f)+g(\lambda x.x\ \&\ y)$$where $\&$ is the Boolean conjunction.
\end{exercise}\par\begin{exercise}Extend the language of type with \emph{products} and that of terms with \emph{tuples} and \emph{projections} and extend the algorithms accordingly.
Check that the term $f(f(1),f(2))$ cannot be typed.
\end{exercise}\par\par\@@unnumbered@section{paragraph}{toc}{Further reading and related work}
Type inference is a central problem in theoretical computer science, starting with the pioneering work of\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/popl/DamasM82}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} in programming languages and\penalty\ \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{10.2307/1995158}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}} in combinatory logic.
The graph-oriented perspective is not common, but has been employed before, for example int the work of \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{DBLP:conf/oopsla/PalsbergS91}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}.
It is unclear whether pursuing this angle can lead to algorithmic improvements and therefore faster times in type inference, but the separation of concerns between collecting and solving constraints seems promising.
At least for pedagogical reasons, we hope it is useful.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Closure conversion}
\par One challenge posed by the compilation of functional languages is the fact that certain operations, for instance partial application of curried functions, seem to lead to the creation of new functions during execution.
For instance, if we write in a generic functional language $\mathit{let}\ f=(\lambda x.\lambda y.x+y)1$ we effectively bound the new function $\lambda y.1+y$ to the variable $f$.
For technical and pragmatic reasons which we shall not delve into here, dealing with the runtime creation of new functions is best avoided.
The ideal situation is that of the programming language C (or its modernised version C++) in which a program consists of a list of functions, all in global scope.
These functions can take other functions as arguments and can return other functions as result, so long as these functions are chosen from the already defined functions.
\par Closure conversion is a transformation that allows the transformation of any program into this desirable form, bringing all functions into global scope.
The 4th ES equation (Definition\penalty\ \ref{def:eseqn}) tells us that in certain condition we can indeed `yank' terms outside an abstraction box:
\par$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam2.pdf}}\put(0.90139,0.10109){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam2.pdf}}\put(0.33021,0.10024){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam2.pdf}}\put(0.1615,0.09899){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam2.pdf}}\put(0.44969,0.09886){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam2.pdf}}\put(0.63676,0.06842){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam2.pdf}}\end{picture}$$However, this law requires the yanked term ($v$) to have no variables bound within the abstraction box it is extracted from.
But how do we extract not $v$ but $u$?
In other words, do we have `adaptor' terms $w$ and $w^{\prime}$ as below so we can do this?
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam3.pdf}}\put(0.29715,0.10478){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam3.pdf}}\put(0.15182,0.10371){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam3.pdf}}\put(0.39861,0.10338){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$=$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam3.pdf}}\put(0.60006,0.13112){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$u$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam3.pdf}}\put(0.7708,0.08527){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam3.pdf}}\put(0.48659,0.10265){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$w$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam3.pdf}}\put(0.89162,0.13236){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$w^{\prime}$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{sbstlam3.pdf}}\end{picture}$$The answer is `not quite, but close enough'.
The first step is to `close' the term that is to be yanked out by treating its free variables as if they were bound variables, then to change applications to take into account these extra arguments.
Once the term is closed, yanking it out of the enclosing abstraction is no longer problematic.
\par Although not strictly necessary, we will use a $\mathit{let}\ x=u\ \mathit{in}v$ binder to define closure conversion.
This is semantically equal to $(\lambda x.v)u$, but we will use this construction to distinguished between thunks created by closure conversion and thunks transformed by closure conversion.
The diagrammatic syntax and operational semantics of the $\mathit{let}$ binder are:
$$\begin{picture}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{let.pdf}}\put(0.30376,0.03066){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$let$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{let.pdf}}\put(0.10896,0.07046){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{let.pdf}}\put(0.76222,0.07046){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{c}$v$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{let.pdf}}\put(0.46217,0.03127){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[lt]{\smash{\begin{tabular}[t]{l}$\rightsquigarrow$\end{tabular}}}}\put(0.0,0.0){\includegraphics[width,page]{let.pdf}}\end{picture}$$\par The transformations, for the terms and for the applications, are given in Figure\penalty\ \ref{fig:closureconv}.
Note that the transformation is not type-preserving as each function type $A\to C$ is replaced by a pair of a closure $B$ and a function with an additional closure argument $A\times B\to C$ .
